title: The Best Coffee Grinder for Beginners
dek: If you only upgrade one thing, upgrade this. Here's which grinder to buy for how you actually brew.
intro: Ask anybody who works a coffee bar what to buy first and you'll hear the same answer: a burr grinder. Not a fancier machine. Not pricier beans. A grinder. Pre-ground coffee goes stale fast, and blade grinders chop beans into dust and boulders that brew unevenly, which is where a lot of 'bitter and sour at the same time' coffee comes from.
A burr grinder crushes beans to a consistent size. That one change makes cheap beans taste better and good beans taste like the bag said they would.
how_we_picked: We focused on grinders a beginner can use on day one, that hold up to daily use, and that come from brands with parts and support. Details come from each product's Amazon listing; check the listing for the current version and price.

picks.verdict: The one we'd hand a friend. Simple, consistent at filter grinds, and repairable for years.
Load the big hopper, set the timer, walk away. Great for households brewing a pot a day.

picks.award: Best if you want espresso too
picks.verdict: One grinder that covers espresso through cold brew. Read recent reviews first; owner ratings are more mixed.

A hand grinder: quiet, portable, and better grind quality than you'd expect for the money.

bar_tip: Grind right before you brew. Ground coffee loses aroma within minutes. Whole beans hold for a few weeks. That gap is the whole reason a grinder matters.

faq.q: Do I really need a burr grinder?
faq.a: If you're happy with your coffee, no. If it's ever bitter, sour, or flat, a burr grinder is the fix that does the most per dollar.

faq.q: Can one grinder do espresso and drip?
faq.a: Some can (the Fellow Opus is built for it), but espresso needs very fine, very small adjustments. Most beginner grinders are tuned for filter coffee.
Hand grinders are quiet and often grind more evenly per dollar, but cranking for a full 10-cup pot gets old. Electric if you brew for a family.
